lessons.title: Deriving the Black-Scholes Partial Differential Equation

children.text: The previous lesson ended one line of algebra short of the finish line: two separate expressions for dΠ, one from the hedge itself, one from no-arbitrage. Set them equal, and something remarkable falls out, not just an equation, but an equation with one very famous variable missing entirely. This lesson finishes that algebra and spends the rest of its time understanding exactly what the result means.

body.text: Setting the hedge's dΠ equal to no-arbitrage's dΠ produces the Black-Scholes partial differential equation, C_t + rS·C_S + (1/2)σ²S²·C_SS = rC. Notice what is not in that equation: μ, the stock's real-world expected return, has vanished completely. The option's fair price never depends on how bullish or bearish the market is about the stock, only on its volatility, the risk-free rate, and time.

children.text: Setting the Two Expressions for dΠ Equal
The previous lesson derived two separate, equally valid expressions for dΠ: one from constructing the hedge and applying Ito's lemma, and one from no-arbitrage alone.

body.latex: \underbrace{-\left[C_t + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 C_{SS}\right] dt}_{\text{from the hedge}} \;=\; \underbrace{r\Pi\, dt = r(-C + C_S S)\, dt}_{\text{from no-arbitrage}}
body.caption: The two expressions for dΠ, set equal

children.text: Divide both sides by dt, distribute the r on the right, and rearrange every term onto one side. Nothing here is a new assumption, it is pure algebra on the two equations already derived.

body.latex: -C_t - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 C_{SS} = -rC + rS\,C_S \quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_t + rS\,C_S + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 S^2 C_{SS} = rC
body.caption: The Black-Scholes partial differential equation

body.text: Scan the final equation for μ. It is nowhere. The μS·C_S term from Ito's lemma and the ΔμS term from the hedge's stock position were exactly equal and cancelled in the previous lesson, before this algebra even started. That cancellation is not a coincidence, it is the entire point of choosing Δ = C_S: the hedge is specifically constructed to neutralize dependence on the stock's actual expected return, leaving only the risk-free rate, r, in its place. Lesson 5 returns to this fact directly, since it is the reason option prices can be computed "as if" every asset earned the risk-free rate, regardless of what investors actually expect the stock to do.

children.text: Reading the Equation Term by Term

body.caption: What each term in the Black-Scholes PDE represents

cells: How the option's value changes purely with the passage of time, holding S fixed
The risk-free drift's contribution, working through the hedge ratio
The contribution from the stock's variance acting on the option's curvature
The return the option's own value must generate to match the riskless rate

children.text: Every one of these four terms lines up with a Greek that appears on any live NSE options chain. This is not a coincidence either: the Greeks are exactly the sensitivities the Black-Scholes PDE is built from, expressed as C_t, C_S, and C_SS.
The Missing Piece: A Boundary Condition

The PDE alone has infinitely many functions C(S, t) that satisfy it; nothing in the equation says which specific option it describes. What pins down a unique solution is a boundary condition: the option's known payoff at expiry, T. For a European call struck at K, that payoff is exactly what the option is worth the instant it expires, its intrinsic value.

body.caption: The terminal (boundary) condition for a European call option

children.text: This combination, a PDE plus a condition known at the end rather than the beginning, is called a terminal value problem, and it is solved by working backward from T to today, t. Crucially, the PDE itself never mentions whether the derivative is a call, a put, or something more exotic; only the boundary condition changes. A European put struck at K would satisfy the exact same PDE, with C(S, T) = max(K - S, 0) as its boundary condition instead.

body.text: This PDE has the same mathematical structure as the heat equation from physics, which describes how temperature diffuses through a material over time. Black and Scholes's original 1973 derivation solved the equation by transforming it, through a change of variables, directly into the heat equation and reusing a known physics solution. The next lesson takes a different, more direct route to the same destination, one that stays inside stochastic calculus rather than borrowing from physics, but the historical connection is part of why this equation is often taught as a landmark bridge between the two fields.

body.title: Identify the missing variable
body.question: Which variable, present in the original stock price SDE, dS = μS dt + σS dW, is completely absent from the final Black-Scholes PDE?
options: μ, the stock's real-world expected return
body.explanation: μ cancelled out exactly during the hedge construction in the previous lesson, since the ΔμS and μS·C_S terms were equal and opposite once Δ = C_S. The PDE depends only on r, σ, S, and t, never on the stock's real-world expected return, a famously counterintuitive result that Lesson 5 explores through the lens of risk-neutral pricing.

body.title: Apply the boundary condition
body.prompt: For a European call option struck at K = ₹4,000, using the boundary condition C(S, T) = max(S - K, 0), what is the option worth at the instant of expiry if the stock is at S = ₹4,300?
body.explanation: C(4300, T) = max(4300 - 4000, 0) = max(300, 0) = ₹300. At expiry, with no time value left, the option is worth exactly its intrinsic value, the amount by which the stock price exceeds the strike.

cards.definition: C_t + rS·C_S + (1/2)σ²S²·C_SS = rC, the equation any European-style option's price must satisfy, derived from a delta-hedged, no-arbitrage portfolio.
The known value of the option at expiry, T, such as C(S,T) = max(S-K,0) for a call; combined with the PDE, it pins down a unique solution.
A differential equation paired with a condition specified at the end of the time interval rather than the start, solved by working backward from expiry to today.

points: Setting the hedge's dΠ equal to no-arbitrage's dΠ and rearranging gives the Black-Scholes PDE: C_t + rS·C_S + (1/2)σ²S²·C_SS = rC.
The stock's real-world expected return, μ, cancels out completely during the hedge construction and never appears in the final PDE, a deliberate consequence of choosing Δ = C_S, not an approximation.
Each term in the PDE corresponds to a Greek seen on a real options chain: C_t to theta, rS·C_S to a delta-driven drift term, and (1/2)σ²S²·C_SS to gamma.
The PDE alone has infinitely many solutions; a specific option's boundary condition, its known payoff at expiry, such as C(S,T) = max(S-K,0) for a call, picks out the one that matters.

The same PDE structure applies to any European-style derivative; only the boundary condition changes, and it shares its mathematical form with the physics heat equation, a historical link the next lesson sets aside in favor of a stochastic-calculus route to the same closed-form solution.
